cards.front: What are the three parts inside a for loop's parentheses, in order?
cards.extra: for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) — set up once, test before each pass, update after each pass. All the loop bookkeeping sits in one line, which is why counting loops prefer for over while.
cards.example:
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { // init; condition; update
    System.out.println(i);
}

cards.front: After int x = 0; int z = x++;, what are x and z?
cards.extra: Post-increment hands over the old value, then increments. ++x increments first, so z would be 1. The difference only matters when the expression's value is used.
cards.example:
int x = 0;
int z = x++;
System.out.println(x + " " + z); // 1 0

cards.front: In an enhanced for loop, what must the iteration variable's type be?
cards.extra: for (String s : names) over a String[]. An int variable over a String[] is a compile error — the variable receives each element, not an index.
cards.example:
String[] names = {"Ann", "Bob"};
for (String s : names) System.out.println(s); // element type
// for (int n : names) { } // error: incompatible types

cards.front: What does the enhanced for loop actually give you over a classic for?
cards.back: A simpler way to walk every element — no index, no counter
cards.extra: It hides the counter and the bounds check, which removes the classic off-by-one. The price is that you cannot skip elements, count by two, or stop at a particular index without a plain loop.
cards.example:
String[] names = {"Ann", "Bob"};
for (String s : names) System.out.println(s); // no index, no counter
for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) System.out.println(names[i]); // classic

cards.front: What does break do inside a loop?
cards.back: Exits the loop immediately, skipping the remaining iterations
cards.extra: Execution continues after the closing brace. In checkYourself() it stops scanning cells as soon as a hit is found — without it the loop would keep comparing and could count the same guess twice.
cards.example:
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  if (i == 2) break;
  System.out.println(i);
}

cards.front: Why write a test class before finishing the real class?
cards.back: To check the behaviour with a known input while the code is still small
cards.extra: The book builds SimpleStartupTestDrive with one guess of 2 and prints "passed" or "failed". Running it immediately is the closest thing to an automated test you get before JUnit.
cards.example:
final class Game { String checkYourself(int guess) { return guess == 2 ? "hit" : "miss"; } }
System.out.println(new Game().checkYourself(2)); // known input -> hit
System.out.println(new Game().checkYourself(3)); // known input -> miss

cards.front: How do you read an integer typed at the command line?
cards.extra: Scanner is in java.util, so it needs an import. nextInt() consumes the next token as an int; it throws if the user types something else.
cards.example:
java.util.Scanner sc = new java.util.Scanner(System.in);
int n = sc.nextInt();
System.out.println(n);

cards.extra: Math.random() returns 0.0 up to but not including 1.0, so multiplying by 5 gives 0.0–4.999…, and the cast truncates. Multiplying by 5 never yields 5.
cards.example:
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    int n = (int) (Math.random() * 5); // 0..4
    System.out.print(n + " ");
}

cards.front: What is the point of writing pseudo-code before Java?
cards.back: It forces the design decisions — what methods exist, what they take, what they return — before syntax gets in the way
cards.extra: The book writes "DECLARE a checkYourself() method that takes an int…" first, then translates line by line. Bugs found at the pseudo-code stage cost nothing to fix.
cards.example:
// DECLARE checkYourself(int guess) -> String "hit" or "miss"
final class Game { String checkYourself(int guess) { return guess == 2 ? "hit" : "miss"; } }
System.out.println(new Game().checkYourself(2)); // hit

cards.front: while (isAlive) { … } with isAlive set false inside the body — what pattern is that?
cards.back: Loop until a state flag flips, not until a counter runs out
cards.extra: The game ends when the last cell is hit, which has nothing to do with how many guesses were made. A boolean flag expresses that condition directly instead of encoding it in a count.
cards.example:
boolean isAlive = true;
while (isAlive) {
    isAlive = false; // last cell hit: a flag flips, not a counter
}

cards.front: Before writing a class, what do you decide first?
cards.back: Its methods: name, parameters, return type — plus what each one does in plain words
cards.extra: The book writes "DECLARE a checkYourself() method that takes an int and returns hit/miss/kill" before any Java exists. Responsibilities first, syntax later — otherwise you design around what is easy to type.
cards.example:
// Decide first: checkYourself(int guess) returns "hit", "miss" or "kill".
final class Game { String checkYourself(int guess) { return guess == 2 ? "hit" : "miss"; } }
System.out.println(new Game().checkYourself(2)); // hit

cards.front: Why does the game class get no test class of its own?
cards.back: It has a single main() — running it is the test
cards.extra: A test class earns its keep when there is behaviour worth calling with known inputs. Here main is the entry point, so the book just plays the game and watches the output.
cards.example:
class Ex { public static void main(String[] args) {
    for (int guess : new int[] {1, 2}) System.out.println(guess == 2 ? "hit" : "miss");
} }

cards.back: A double from 0.0 up to but never including 1.0
cards.extra: That half-open range is why (int)(Math.random() * n) covers 0…n−1 exactly, and why it can never return n.
cards.example:
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    double d = Math.random(); // 0.0 <= d < 1.0
    System.out.println(d);
}
